BARCELONA, Spain (CNN) -- Google launched the latest salvo in the cellphone wars Tuesday with the unveiling of the newest handset to carry its Android platform. Google's Android platform goes head to head with Apple's iPhone. Unveiled at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, Vodafone's HTC Magic smartphone will make its European bow in the UK, Spain, France and Germany in the coming months. In Italy it will be available under a non-exclusive contract. The Google-run handsets are regarded as the chief rivals to Apple's iPhones in the battle for the next generation of mobile devices. Google's latest foray into the cell phone market is seen by many as the beginnings of the Internet giant's attempts to dominate the industry. Some have expressed concerns that cell phone manufacturers, network operators and users will have little control over what data Google will be able to utilise from its software. Among critics is the LiMo Foundation, representing Linux-based operating system LiMo, which has launched its own cell phone platform, according to Congress organizer Groupe Speciale Mobile Association's daily newsletter. "A lot of operators still harbor some questions over whether they will have the control over services and how much of the data that is going out and coming from a Google device goes to Google and how much to you [the operator]," LiMo's Andrew Shikiar told Mobile Business Briefing. Users of both the Apple and Google models can download applications developed by third-parties from open-source software, potentially giving them the capability of small handheld computers. The first Android-capable handset, the G1, was launched last year. It partnered with T-Mobile for its UK launch, its first foray into the European market. The HTC Magic includes a 3.2-inch QVGA touch screen display, navigational buttons and a trackball. It also comes with several Google applications including Google Mail, Google Maps and Google Search as well as YouTube, which is owned by Google. Andy Rubin, Senior Director of Mobile Platforms at Google, said that the launch of the HTC Magic was an important step for Android. "With it, Vodafone is opening up the mobile web for consumers across Europe and giving more third-party developers a platform on which they can build the next wave of killer applications," Rubin said. CNN's Adrian Finighan, who is at the congress, said that as an iPhone user he had spent much of his time at this year's event looking for something to rival his device. "The Magic is, well, magic! I think I've found it. It really is the first device that I could consider swapping my beloved Apple device for."

outputs.L1:
BARCELONA, Spain (CNN) — Google launched the latest salvo in the cellphone wars Tuesday, unveiling the newest handset to carry its Android platform. Google’s Android platform goes head to head with Apple’s iPhone.

Introduced at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, Vodafone’s HTC Magic smartphone will make its European debut in the UK, Spain, France and Germany in the coming months. In Italy, it will be available under a non-exclusive contract.

The Google-run handsets are widely regarded as the chief rivals to Apple’s iPhones in the battle for the next generation of mobile devices. Google’s latest foray into the cellphone market is seen by many as the beginning of the Internet giant’s attempt to dominate the industry.

Some have expressed concerns that cellphone manufacturers, network operators and users will have little control over what data Google will be able to utilize through its software. Among the critics is the LiMo Foundation, representing the Linux-based operating system LiMo, which has launched its own cellphone platform, according to the daily newsletter of Congress organizer Groupe Speciale Mobile Association.

“A lot of operators still harbor some questions over whether they will have control over services, and how much of the data that is going out and coming from a Google device goes to Google and how much to you [the operator],” LiMo’s Andrew Shikiar told Mobile Business Briefing.

Users of both the Apple and Google models can download applications developed by third parties from open-source software, potentially giving the devices the capabilities of small handheld computers.

The first Android-capable handset, the G1, was launched last year. It partnered with T-Mobile for its UK launch, marking its first foray into the European market.

The HTC Magic includes a 3.2-inch QVGA touchscreen display, navigational buttons and a trackball. It also comes with several Google applications, including Google Mail, Google Maps and Google Search, as well as YouTube, which is owned by Google.

Andy Rubin, Senior Director of Mobile Platforms at Google, said the launch of the HTC Magic was an important step for Android.

“With it, Vodafone is opening up the mobile web for consumers across Europe and giving more third-party developers a platform on which they can build the next wave of killer applications,” Rubin said.

CNN’s Adrian Finighan, who is at the congress, said that, as an iPhone user, he had spent much of his time at this year’s event looking for something to rival his device.

“The Magic is, well, magic! I think I’ve found it. It really is the first device that I could consider swapping my beloved Apple device for.”

BARCELONA, Spain (CNN) — Google made a fresh move in the mobile phone rivalry on Tuesday by introducing the newest device built to run on its Android operating system.

Android is positioned as a direct competitor to Apple’s iPhone. The new handset, Vodafone’s HTC Magic smartphone, was presented at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Europe first in the UK, Spain, France and Germany over the next few months. In Italy, the phone will be offered through a non-exclusive agreement.

Phones powered by Google’s software are widely seen as the main challengers to Apple’s iPhone in the race to shape the next generation of mobile technology. Many observers view Google’s expanding presence in the handset market as an early sign of the Internet company’s ambition to become a dominant force in the sector.

However, some critics have raised questions about how much influence mobile phone makers, network operators and customers will have over the information Google can access through its software. One of those voicing concern is the LiMo Foundation, which represents the Linux-based LiMo operating system and has introduced its own mobile platform, according to a daily newsletter from Congress organizer Groupe Speciale Mobile Association.

“A lot of operators still harbor some questions over whether they will have the control over services and how much of the data that is going out and coming from a Google device goes to Google and how much to you [the operator],” LiMo’s Andrew Shikiar told Mobile Business Briefing.

Both Apple and Google handset users are able to download third-party applications created using open-source software, giving the devices the potential to function like compact handheld computers.

The first phone capable of running Android, the G1, was released the previous year. For its UK debut, and Google’s first step into the European mobile market, it was launched in partnership with T-Mobile.

The HTC Magic features a 3.2-inch QVGA touchscreen, navigation keys and a trackball. It also includes a range of Google services, such as Google Mail, Google Maps and Google Search, along with YouTube, which is also owned by Google.

Andy Rubin, Google’s Senior Director of Mobile Platforms, described the HTC Magic launch as a significant milestone for Android.

“With it, Vodafone is opening up the mobile web for consumers across Europe and giving more third-party developers a platform on which they can build the next wave of killer applications,” Rubin said.

CNN’s Adrian Finighan, reporting from the congress, said that as an iPhone owner he had spent much of the event searching for a device that could compete with his own.

“The Magic is, well, magic! I think I’ve found it. It really is the first device that I could consider swapping my beloved Apple device for.”

Google stepped up its challenge to Apple’s iPhone at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona with the unveiling of the HTC Magic, a new smartphone running on the company’s Android operating system and backed by Vodafone for launch in several European markets.

The device, manufactured by Taiwan’s HTC, represents one of the most significant European rollouts yet for Android, the mobile software platform Google has positioned as an open alternative to the tightly controlled systems used by rivals such as Apple. Vodafone said the HTC Magic would be introduced in key markets including Britain, Spain, Germany, France and Italy, giving Google a broader opportunity to place its services directly in the hands of mobile users.

The launch highlights the growing importance of software and internet services in the next generation of mobile devices. Rather than competing only on hardware design, handset makers and technology companies are increasingly focused on the applications, search tools, maps, email and online services that shape how consumers use their phones. Android is central to Google’s strategy because it allows the company to extend its search, advertising and web services beyond desktop computers and into the rapidly expanding mobile market.

The HTC Magic is expected to compete directly with other advanced smartphones, particularly Apple’s iPhone, which has set the standard for touch-screen devices and mobile applications. Like the iPhone, the Magic is designed around a large touch screen and easy access to the internet. It also offers close integration with Google services such as Gmail, Google Maps and search, making it a showcase for the company’s broader mobile ambitions.

For Vodafone, the partnership offers a way to strengthen its smartphone lineup and compete with operators that have benefited from exclusive or high-profile iPhone deals. By supporting an Android-based handset, Vodafone can offer customers an alternative device with strong internet features while aligning itself with one of the world’s most powerful technology companies.

However, the rise of Android is also prompting concern among mobile operators and competitors. While Android is promoted as an open platform, Google’s growing influence over mobile services raises questions about who controls the relationship with users and who has access to valuable data generated by mobile activity. Operators have traditionally relied on customer data, billing relationships and service offerings as central parts of their business. Google’s ability to gather information through search, location services, email and applications could shift more power away from network operators and toward internet companies.

Competitors are also watching Android’s expansion closely. If the platform gains significant market share, Google could become a dominant force not only in mobile search and advertising but also in the broader smartphone ecosystem. That prospect has intensified the rivalry between Google, Apple, Microsoft, Nokia and other companies seeking to define the future of mobile computing.

The unveiling of the HTC Magic therefore marks more than the arrival of another handset. It signals Android’s emergence as a serious contender in the smartphone market and reinforces the growing battle between technology companies and mobile operators for control of the mobile internet.

**BARCELONA, Spain (CNN) —** Google and Vodafone unveiled the HTC Magic at Mobile World Congress in Barcelona on Tuesday, marking the Internet giant’s latest push to bring its Android mobile operating system to European consumers and intensifying its rivalry with Apple’s iPhone.

The sleek, touch-screen handset — built by Taiwan’s HTC and sold by Vodafone — is the second major phone to run Google’s Android software, following the T-Mobile G1. Unlike the G1, the HTC Magic does not include a slide-out physical keyboard, relying instead on a virtual keyboard and a thinner, more iPhone-like design.

Vodafone said the HTC Magic would launch first in Europe, with rollouts planned for the United Kingdom, Spain, Germany, France and Italy in the spring. The company also said it expected the phone to be introduced in other Vodafone markets later, as Android gains broader support from manufacturers and carriers.

Google’s vice president of engineering, Andy Rubin, who leads the Android project, said the device reflected the company’s effort to make mobile Internet access more open and widely available.

“People want the same Internet experience on their phones that they have on their computers,” Rubin said at the Barcelona event. “Android was designed to give manufacturers, operators and developers the freedom to innovate quickly.”

The HTC Magic comes with Google services built in, including Gmail, Google Maps, Google Search and YouTube. It also offers access to Android Market, Google’s application store, where users can download third-party software — a key battleground as mobile platforms compete to attract developers.

The launch comes as smartphone makers and wireless carriers try to catch up with Apple, whose iPhone has reshaped consumer expectations for mobile devices since its debut. With its large touch screen, app ecosystem and tight integration of hardware and software, the iPhone remains the benchmark for many users.

But Google’s strategy differs sharply from Apple’s. Rather than building its own handset and tightly controlling the user experience, Google is offering Android as an open-source platform that can be adapted by multiple manufacturers and operators.

That openness, however, has raised questions across the mobile industry. Members of the LiMo Foundation — a rival group promoting a Linux-based mobile platform — have warned that Android may not be as open as advertised if Google services and commercial priorities dominate the experience.

LiMo representatives and other industry observers have also pointed to privacy and control concerns, noting that Android devices are deeply tied to Google accounts and online services. As smartphones collect more location, search and personal data, critics say consumers need clearer assurances about who controls that information and how it is used.

CNN’s Adrian Finighan, reporting from Mobile World Congress, said the HTC Magic underscored how quickly the smartphone market was shifting.

“This is no longer just about making calls,” Finighan said. “It’s about who controls the mobile Internet experience — the handset maker, the network operator, the software company or the consumer.”

Rubin rejected the idea that Android was designed to lock users into Google, saying the platform’s open-source foundation would encourage competition and choice.

“The goal is not to control the phone,” Rubin said. “The goal is to create an open platform that lets the best ideas reach consumers.”

For Vodafone, the HTC Magic offers a chance to challenge the iPhone in markets where Apple’s device has generated intense interest but remains tied to selected carriers. By backing Android, Vodafone gains a high-profile smartphone with access to Google’s growing ecosystem — and a way to differentiate itself in a crowded market.

Analysts say the success of the HTC Magic will depend not only on its hardware and pricing, but also on whether Android Market can grow quickly enough to rival Apple’s App Store. Apple’s head start in applications remains significant, but Google’s brand, developer reach and search-driven services give Android strong momentum.

At Mobile World Congress, where handset makers and carriers are searching for the next major growth engine, the HTC Magic’s debut signaled that Android is no longer an experiment limited to one device or one market.

Whether it can become a true iPhone rival in Europe will depend on consumers — and on how comfortable they are with Google playing an increasingly central role in their mobile lives.

**BARCELONA, Spain, Feb. 17 —** Google’s push into the mobile phone market gathered pace in Europe on Tuesday as HTC and Vodafone unveiled the **HTC Magic**, the latest handset to run Google’s Android operating system and the first major Android phone aimed squarely at European consumers.

Introduced at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, the HTC Magic is a slimmer, touch-screen successor to the T-Mobile G1, the first Android handset launched last year in the United States and Britain. Unlike the G1, the Magic drops the slide-out physical keyboard in favor of an all-touch design, bringing it visually closer to Apple’s iPhone — the device that has reshaped consumer expectations for smartphones.

Vodafone said it would sell the HTC Magic in several European markets, including Britain, Spain, Germany and France, with availability expected in the spring. The device features a 3.2-inch touch screen, a 3.2-megapixel camera, GPS, Wi-Fi and access to the Android Market, Google’s online store for mobile applications.

The launch marks an important step for Google, which is seeking to establish Android as a broad software platform for many manufacturers and carriers rather than a single branded device. While Apple tightly controls both the iPhone hardware and software, Google is pursuing a more open model, giving handset makers and network operators greater freedom to customize Android phones and services.

That difference is increasingly central to the emerging smartphone rivalry. Apple’s iPhone has built a powerful lead in mobile browsing, music, media and downloadable applications through its App Store. Google, by contrast, is betting that Android’s openness — combined with its search, maps, Gmail and advertising services — will encourage a wider range of devices and faster adoption across carriers around the world.

The HTC Magic is also a sign that Android is moving beyond its early-adopter phase. The G1 was widely viewed as a promising but somewhat bulky first effort, appealing especially to users who wanted a physical keyboard and close integration with Google services. The Magic’s sleeker form factor suggests that Android handset makers are now targeting mainstream consumers who have been drawn to the iPhone’s simplicity and touch-based interface.

Still, Google and its partners face a formidable competitor. Apple has a strong brand, a mature applications ecosystem and a loyal customer base. The iPhone’s integration with iTunes and its polished user experience remain key advantages. Android, meanwhile, must prove that multiple manufacturers and operators can deliver consistent quality without fragmenting the user experience.

For Vodafone, the HTC Magic offers a way to compete more directly against operators carrying the iPhone and to participate in the fast-growing market for data-heavy smartphones. Mobile operators are increasingly looking to smartphones to drive revenue from internet access, email, navigation and downloadable software as voice-call growth slows.

Industry executives in Barcelona said the smartphone contest is no longer just about hardware specifications. It is increasingly a battle of platforms: Apple’s iPhone OS, Google’s Android, Nokia’s Symbian, Research in Motion’s BlackBerry and Microsoft’s Windows Mobile are all competing to attract developers, carriers and consumers.

The HTC Magic gives Google a more attractive vehicle for that fight. Whether it can seriously dent Apple’s momentum will depend not only on the handset’s design and pricing, but also on how quickly Android Market fills with compelling applications — and whether Google’s open approach can produce the same kind of excitement Apple has generated around the iPhone.

# Google’s Android Push in Europe Gathers Pace with the HTC Magic

Google’s ambitions in mobile computing took a significant step forward in Europe with the arrival of the HTC Magic, a sleek touchscreen smartphone that brought the company’s Android platform to a wider international audience. Backed by Vodafone, one of the world’s largest mobile operators, the Magic marked an important moment in Android’s early expansion beyond its first commercial handset, the T-Mobile G1.

The launch signaled that Android was no longer an experimental challenger confined to a single device or market. Instead, it was beginning to emerge as a serious platform for handset makers, operators, developers, and consumers looking for an alternative to Apple’s iPhone and other established smartphone systems.

## From the G1 to the HTC Magic

Android made its commercial debut in 2008 with the T-Mobile G1, also known as the HTC Dream. Released first in the United States and later in parts of Europe, the G1 was manufactured by HTC and sold through T-Mobile. It introduced consumers to Google’s mobile operating system, including deep integration with Gmail, Google Maps, search, contacts, and the Android Market, Google’s early app store.

The G1 was an important proof of concept, but it was also a somewhat unconventional device. It featured a slide-out physical keyboard, a trackball, and a relatively bulky design. While it appealed to early adopters and Google enthusiasts, it lacked the polish and simplicity that had helped Apple’s iPhone capture mainstream attention.

The HTC Magic represented a refinement of that first Android effort. It dropped the physical keyboard in favor of a thinner, fully touchscreen design, making it more directly comparable to the iPhone. Also built by HTC, the Magic retained Google’s services at its core while presenting Android in a more consumer-friendly form.

## Vodafone’s Key Role in Android’s European Expansion

Vodafone’s involvement was central to the HTC Magic’s significance. As a major international carrier with a strong presence across Europe, Vodafone gave Android access to a much broader customer base than the G1 had initially enjoyed.

The Magic was introduced across several European markets, including the United Kingdom, Spain, Germany, France, and Italy, depending on Vodafone’s local rollout plans and partnerships. By placing Android in its retail stores, marketing campaigns, and subscription offerings, Vodafone helped move the platform from niche curiosity to mainstream contender.

For mobile operators, Android offered an attractive strategic opportunity. The iPhone had strengthened Apple’s influence over the customer experience, software ecosystem, and services layered on top of the network. Android, by contrast, promised a more open and flexible model. Operators could support a modern smartphone platform without ceding as much control to a single hardware and software company.

Vodafone’s support also suggested confidence that Android could become a viable counterweight to Apple, Nokia’s Symbian, Research In Motion’s BlackBerry platform, Microsoft’s Windows Mobile, and other systems then competing for mobile users.

## Taking Aim at the iPhone

The HTC Magic arrived at a time when the iPhone had dramatically reshaped expectations for smartphones. Apple’s device had set a new standard for mobile web browsing, touch interfaces, app distribution, and design simplicity. Competing platforms were under pressure to match not only the iPhone’s hardware appeal but also its growing ecosystem of applications.

Android’s pitch was different. Rather than being tied to one manufacturer and one tightly controlled product line, Android was designed as an open platform that could be used by multiple handset makers and operators. Google’s strategy depended on scale: the more manufacturers that adopted Android, the more devices would reach the market, attracting more developers and ultimately more users.

The HTC Magic was one of the first clear signs of that strategy in action. Its touchscreen form factor made it easier to compare directly with the iPhone, while its integration with Google services gave it a distinct identity. Features such as push Gmail, Google Maps, web search, YouTube access, and the Android Market helped position the device as a cloud-connected smartphone built around Google’s internet services.

However, Android still faced challenges. The iPhone had a more mature app ecosystem, strong brand recognition, and a reputation for ease of use. Android, while promising, was still young. Its interface and application selection were developing, and early devices had to prove they could compete not only on features but also on usability, design, and battery life.

## Industry Reaction: Cautious Optimism

Reaction from the mobile industry was generally one of cautious optimism. Many analysts and executives saw Android’s expansion as a necessary development in a market increasingly shaped by software platforms rather than just hardware specifications.

For handset manufacturers such as HTC, Android provided a way to reduce dependence on older smartphone operating systems and participate in a growing ecosystem backed by Google’s brand and technical resources. HTC had already played a crucial role in producing both the G1 and the Magic, positioning itself as one of Android’s earliest and most important hardware partners.

Operators viewed Android as a way to diversify their smartphone portfolios. The success of the iPhone had shown that high-end data devices could drive mobile internet usage and increase demand for data plans. But it also created concern among carriers that Apple could dominate the customer relationship. Android gave operators another premium smartphone option while preserving more room for customization, pricing flexibility, and service bundling.

Developers, meanwhile, were watching closely. Android Market was still young compared with Apple’s App Store, but the promise of an open platform appealed to many software creators. A broader device rollout across Europe meant a larger potential audience for Android applications.

Some industry observers warned that openness could also create complications. If multiple manufacturers and operators customized Android in different ways, the platform risked fragmentation, making it harder for developers to ensure consistent performance across devices. Even in Android’s early days, this tension between openness and consistency was already visible.

## A Turning Point for Android

The HTC Magic did not instantly overturn the smartphone market, nor did it immediately threaten the iPhone’s cultural momentum. But its importance lay in what it represented: Android was expanding beyond its first device, gaining support from a major global carrier, and entering key European markets with a more refined handset.

In retrospect, the Magic was part of the foundation for Android’s rapid rise. It helped demonstrate that Google’s mobile operating system could work across different devices and commercial partnerships. It also showed that operators and manufacturers were eager for a platform that could compete in the new app-centric smartphone era.

The European rollout through Vodafone gave Android visibility, credibility, and distribution at a crucial stage. As more manufacturers later adopted the platform, Android would evolve from a newcomer into the world’s most widely used mobile operating system.

The HTC Magic was therefore more than just the second Android phone. It was an early sign that Google’s mobile strategy was beginning to scale—and that the battle for the future of smartphones would not belong to Apple alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a journalistic report on the unveiling of the HTC Magic smartphone at the Barcelona Mobile World Congress, focusing on Android’s challenge to the iPhone, operator concerns, third-party apps, and quotes from Google and a CNN correspondent.
counterfactuals.output:
**BARCELONA, Spain —** HTC and Vodafone used the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona to unveil the **HTC Magic**, the second major handset built on Google’s Android operating system and the first Android device aimed squarely at a broad European audience.

Sleeker than the earlier T-Mobile G1 and dispensing with a physical keyboard, the Magic was presented as a sign that Android was moving beyond its first experimental phase and into direct competition with Apple’s iPhone. With a large touchscreen, web-centric interface and tight integration with Google services such as Gmail, Maps and Search, the phone underscored Google’s ambition to make Android a mainstream mobile platform rather than a single-device novelty.

A Google representative at the event framed the launch as part of a wider strategy: **“Android is about openness — giving operators, manufacturers and developers the ability to innovate on top of a common platform.”** The message was clear: where Apple controls both the iPhone hardware experience and the App Store ecosystem, Google is betting that multiple handset makers and networks can build a broader challenge.

That approach has attracted strong interest from mobile operators, but also anxiety. Carriers at the Barcelona show privately and publicly questioned whether Android would strengthen their role or further shift power toward internet companies. Operators have long worried about becoming “dumb pipes” — providers of data connections while companies such as Google, Apple and Facebook control the customer relationship, advertising revenue and services layered on top.

The Magic’s launch highlighted those tensions. Vodafone gained a high-profile device to compete with the iPhone in several European markets, but Android’s deep links to Google also raised questions about branding, revenue sharing and control over applications.

Third-party software was another major focus. Android Market, Google’s answer to Apple’s App Store, was central to the pitch. Developers can create applications for the platform with fewer restrictions than Apple’s tightly curated model, a difference Google and HTC portrayed as a competitive advantage. The availability of independent apps — from mapping and messaging tools to games and productivity software — is increasingly seen as decisive in the smartphone race.

A CNN correspondent covering the congress captured the broader industry mood, noting that **“the iPhone changed what consumers expect from a mobile phone; Android is Google’s attempt to make sure that future is not controlled by one company.”**

The HTC Magic may not immediately match the iPhone’s polish or cultural momentum, but its unveiling in Barcelona signaled that the battle over the smartphone market was widening. Apple had proved the appeal of the touchscreen internet phone. Google’s Android, backed by HTC, Vodafone and a growing developer community, was now positioning itself as the open alternative — and operators were watching carefully to see whether that openness would empower them or leave them with less control than before.
